issues.item: Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, hypervigilance can be coherent, but specifically scanning for weapons or dangerous objects points to an interpersonal/assaultive threat context rather than chemical contamination. This threat item is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type and with the memory items, which are sensory and exposure-based rather than assault-related.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Sexual Coping: I release my tension with sexual fantasies/ activities
issues.explanation: Sexual coping is not impossible, but here it is weakly anchored to the rest of the profile. The active formulation is dominated by Memory–Threat–Maladaptive Strategies links around re-experiencing and danger, while the other strategy items are broad avoidance/denial. This item addresses tension reduction in a way not otherwise represented by the triggers, threat, or memory content, making the profile less clinically coherent.

vignette:
Priya's Unraveling

Priya Desai had spent twenty-three years in the Foreign Service, negotiating trade agreements and representing American interests in posts across three continents. She was competent, composed, and accustomed to managing crises. Then came the chemical leak at the embassy compound in Tbilisi.

It was late afternoon when the alarm sounded. The facility manager had discovered a ruptured containment vessel in the basement—industrial solvents used for equipment maintenance, their acrid smell already creeping through the ventilation system. Priya was in her office on the fourth floor when the evacuation order came. She made it down three flights of stairs before the fumes thickened, and she found herself breathing through her sleeve, her eyes watering, that metallic taste coating her tongue—sharp and chemical, almost like burnt copper mixed with something synthetic and wrong. She was among the last out, and by the time she reached the courtyard, her lungs burned and her vision had begun to blur. The hospital visit that followed, the chest X-rays, the reassurance that her lungs would recover—all of it felt distant now, a bureaucratic afterthought to the real injury, which was something she could not quite name.

Three months had passed since the evacuation, and Priya had returned to Washington on medical leave. She told herself the event had not really been that bad, that her body had overreacted, that thousands of people were exposed to worse chemicals every day without falling apart. This reassurance worked for a few weeks. Then the intrusions began.

A colleague microwaved fish in the office break room, and the smell—not even similar, really, but something about its pungency—sent Priya spiraling. The memory arrived without warning, complete and overwhelming: the taste of the solvent coating her mouth, the burn in her sinuses, the press of bodies in the stairwell. Her hands shook as she gathered her things and left early, telling no one why. She began avoiding the break room entirely, timing her lunch to avoid any chance of encountering food smells. She stopped attending embassy events, declined invitations to restaurants, and eventually resigned from the weekly policy committee that met in a windowless conference room—the air felt too still there, and she was certain she could smell something chemical in the recycled atmosphere. What had started as a reasonable precaution had calcified into a rigid system of avoidance that now governed her days.

The more Priya avoided triggers, the more fragile her sense of safety became. She could not go to the grocery store without scanning the cleaning supplies aisle—her body tensing, her pulse quickening, her mind cataloging every potential hazard. She found herself irritable with her sister, snapping at her over nothing, her anger disproportionate and immediate. Her body felt as though it were perpetually braced for danger, muscles tight across her shoulders and chest, her breath shallow and controlled. This constant vigilance exhausted her, and the exhaustion made her more vulnerable to the intrusions. When she tried to distract herself by thinking of other things, she found she could not; the moment she relaxed her guard, the memory returned with renewed force. The taste would bloom on her tongue—that metallic, acrid sensation—and with it came the full sensory flood: the fumes, the fear, the conviction that her body was being poisoned from within.

Priya had begun to avoid anything that felt remotely stressful, believing that emotional strain might somehow trigger another exposure or weaken her already compromised system. She turned down a promotion. She stopped seeing friends who asked difficult questions. She spent her evenings alone in her apartment, the windows sealed, the air purifier running constantly—a white noise that she had come to depend on, a barrier between herself and an increasingly threatening world. The irony was not lost on her: in trying to protect herself from the memory, she had made it more powerful. The avoidance had become its own kind of toxin, and now, six months after the leak, she found herself wondering if she would ever feel safe enough to leave her apartment again.
